In Forest Shuffle, 2-5 players compete in gathering the most valuable trees and attract species, thus creating an ecologically balanced habitat for flora and fauna. It all starts with a single tree: Each turn you play cards from your hand. You want to gather more trees in your very own forest. To help attract wildlife, you try to combine plants and animals for extra points or bonus actions. Consider the different preferences of these creatures: Some animals feel only comfortable in the presence of their fellow species, others prefer certain tree types to live in. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn Actions 3 Cards 4 Game End Overview In Forest Shuffle you create a habitat for flora and fauna to thrive. Plant trees and synergize your cards to earn the most points before winter. Turn Actions Choose between one of two options: 1) Draw two cards from the clearing and/or deck and add them to your hand. ~ Your hand limit is 10 cards. You can't take the draw action if you already have 10 cards. If you have 9 cards, you may only draw 1 card. 2) Play one card from your hand: pay its cost by discarding cards from your hand, then place the chosen card in the forest and carry out its effect. ~ If your discard causes there to be 10 or more cards in the clearing, all cards in the clearing are removed at the end of the turn. BONUS ACTION: Some cards give a special effect if ALL of the cards you pay with show the matching leaf symbol. The bonus action and required symbols will be on the bottom left of the card. On split cards, only one half of the card must bear the symbol. Cards There are 3 types of cards: Trees, Forest Dwellers, and Winter. TREE CARDS depict a single Tree. To plant a tree in the forest, simply pay its cost. The cost amount shown in the brown rectangle at the top left of the card. To pay it, place a number of cards from your hand into the clearing equal to the cost. ~ Trees cards provide a slot on each side (top, bottom, left, right) for you to add forest dwellers. Only 1 forest dweller per slot, unless the card says otherwise. ~ Each time you play a tree, a card from the deck is added to the Clearing. ~ Note that ANY card in your hand may be placed face-down in the forest as a TREE SAPLING. These work exactly like a tree but do not belong to a tree species. FOREST DWELLER CARDS are split. They depict two creatures on them, but only ONE of them may be played. These are the animals, plants, insects and mushrooms that you can add to the forest. ~ To play a forest dweller, select an empty slot on a tree for the desired half of the card, then discard cards from your hand into the clearing equal to the cost. ~ Once a forest dweller is slotted onto a tree, the other half of the card is now hidden. Only the effects of the visible forest dweller may trigger. WINTER CARDS: When you have drawn the top 2/3rds of the deck the first WINTER CARD will be revealed. The other two WINTER CARDS were previously shuffled into the remainder of the deck and serve as a random end timer. When the 3rd winter card is drawn, the game ends immediately! You may not finish your turn. Game End Total the points of all visible cards in your forests, plus one point per card you hid in your cave (if any). None of their effects trigger. The player with the most points wins! In Forest Shuffle, players compete to gather the most valuable trees, then attract species to these trees, thus creating an ecologically balanced habitat for flora and fauna.

To start, each player has six cards in hand, with cards depicting either a particular type of tree or two forest dwellers (animal, plant, mushroom, etc.), with these latter cards being divided in half, whether vertically or horizontally, with one dweller in each card half.

On a turn, either draw two cards — whether face down from the deck or face up from the clearing — and add them to your hand, or play a card from your hand by paying the cost, then putting it into play.

During set-up, three winter cards were placed into the bottom third of the deck. When the third winter card is drawn, the game ends immediately, then players tally their points based on the trees and dwellers in their forest. Whoever scores the most points wins.

Manufactured from FSC-certified material.

[Rating: 1/10] Not really for me. Abhor the randomness of the cards and how swingy (and sometimes restrictive) the scoring can be.

[Rating: 1/10] A point salad tableau builder. It naturally invites combos to get bonus turns, set points, more cards etc.  +Art and layout looks good on table –Deer+predators seem overpowered, especially deer once you get a few deer your points can skyrocket –Low interaction –Game has a random immediate ending (like Ethnos the draw 3 dragon/winter cards). This could be unsatisfying, in Ethnos it worked wdue to the area majority scoring on the board –40-60 minutes is too long for this type of game. RftG is 15-20 minutes and miles better than Forest Shuffle.  Honestly for something akin to this but easier than

[Rating: 1/10] There's a little bit of interaction here, messing with the tableau, but it feels drowned out by optimizing your trees in all directions. Too much attention needed downward to look at other players. I had some unexpected enjoyment in finding that some animals score ridiculously well, so much that it's not really a close race, but not enough to justify the rest of the design. I almost wish the game could just be focused on the aspects I did like, but "Deer Shuffle" might not sell as well.

[Rating: 1/10] The worst game I ever played. Boring, boring not rewarding the time spend on it. At the end you count neverending relations between cards.

[Rating: 2/10] Yuck. Super loose and random. Baked-in synergies with seemingly little room for any kind of tactics. The most you can do is hoard cards and then try to shed out as fast as possible to force the middle to cycle. The strategies are too coherent and don't present you with overlapping tradeoffs or next paths like a game such as Race might. It's a relatively simple game strategically yet it comes off as very intimidating and AP inducing. Very skeptical about the balance of the strategies. What an odd game.

[Rating: 2/10] After my first play, I thought the game was good but not great. The problem arose when I discovered that the strategy I was following was pretty broken — and there was an even more egregious one. Unplayable.

[Rating: 2/10] Nature-themed tableau builder about comboing cards to score points: could it get more in tune with the BGG zeitgeist?  The game uses the pay-for-cards-with-other-cards system seen in games like Race for the Galaxy, except the cards you play are discarded into a central area, from which players can also draw. Whilst it's satisfying to play an extra-turn-granting combo and reclaim cards you had seemingly "spent" in order to use them again, that's about it really and I didn't think it added anything to the formula. [Rating: 2/10] Way too long, too much a table hog, and too straight forward with just straight forward fishing for the right cards. Just not that interesting gameplay - no puzzle to figure out. No engine to build and run. Really fell flat for me.
